text: In the kickoff we framed two questions, generated an illustrative messy orders file, audited it, and wrote a cleaning plan. Now we execute: turn the plan into tested code, produce a clean dataset, and answer both questions with numbers and a chart. Every figure below comes from our illustrative dataset, generated with seed 42.

Each item in the plan becomes one function in cleaning dot p y: drop_duplicate_rows, standardize_text, parse_types, filter_quantity, handle_discount, and add_revenue, chained together by clean_orders. The date trick is worth noting — we parse the whole column with each format using errors equals coerce, so failures become NaT, then fillna combines the two results, so every date matches exactly one format.

We wrote three tests in all: one for date and price parsing, one for the quantity filter — confirming it drops missing, zero, negative, and absurdly large values while keeping 1 and 5 — and one on the real file asserting unique order IDs, no missing dates, and positive revenue. All three passed.

Running the pipeline and counting rows: 1,530 raw rows, 1,500 after removing duplicates, 1,442 after the quantity rule. Of those, 74 rows have a flagged missing discount, and dates now span all of 2024. Always report how many rows your cleaning removed — losing about 4% of the deduplicated rows to the quantity rule deserves a sentence in your write-up.

Grouping completed orders by region, category, and month: North leads at about $50,958, followed by East, West, and South. Electronics generates the most revenue — $62,979 from just 182 orders — because its average order is about $346, while Apparel has the most orders but a much lower average. Monthly revenue jumps sharply in October, November, and December — Q4 is 34.6% of annual revenue, though it's only 25% of the calendar.

For the discount question, we band orders by discount percentage and compare average quantity and return rate across bands. Average quantity per order is flat at roughly three items in every band, so on this data discounts aren't making customers buy more per order. Return rates run from 7.2% at no discount up to 12.6% at 21 to 30% off — higher in discounted bands, but the deepest band has only 103 orders, so call this a lead worth testing, not proof.

Finally, a chart: matplotlib turns the monthly revenue series into a bar chart in the house crimson color, titled and labeled, saved to reports slash monthly_revenue dot png at 150 dpi. The saved chart makes the Q4 surge obvious at a glance — code you can rerun any time the data changes.

To recap: each cleaning decision became a small tested function, chained with dot pipe. We tracked rows through the funnel — 1,530, 1,500, 1,442. Revenue is concentrated in the North, in Electronics, and in Q4. Discounts didn't raise items per order, and returns were higher in discounted bands, a lead to investigate carefully. Next, we wrap up: turning these findings into a presentation and a portfolio piece.
